title: Organisation of the Human Body
description: Cells, tissues, organs, and systems — how the body is built

concepts.title: Hierarchy of Organisation
concepts.contentHtml:
The human body is organised in a hierarchy: atoms → molecules → organelles → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.

Each level has emergent properties not present at the level below. A muscle cell has proteins that can contract; a tissue has coordinated contraction; a muscle organ produces force; the muscular system enables movement.

The body has about 37 trillion cells of ~200 distinct types. These are organised into four tissue types: epithelial (covers surfaces), connective (supports and binds), muscle (contracts), and nervous (transmits signals).

concepts.title: Homeostasis
concepts.contentHtml:
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes. Walter Cannon coined the term in 1926. Almost every organ system contributes to homeostasis.

Homeostatic systems typically use negative feedback: a change in a variable triggers a response that counteracts the change. Body temperature is maintained at ~37°C: if you overheat, blood vessels dilate and sweat glands activate to cool you. If you get cold, blood vessels constrict and muscles shiver to generate heat.

When homeostasis fails, disease results. Type 2 diabetes is a failure of blood glucose homeostasis — cells stop responding normally to insulin, and glucose stays dangerously elevated.

concepts.title: The Eleven Organ Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
The human body has eleven organ systems:

  • Integumentary — skin, hair, nails (protection, thermoregulation)
  • Skeletal — bones, cartilage (support, movement, haematopoiesis)
  • Muscular — skeletal, cardiac, smooth muscle (movement, posture)
  • Nervous — brain, spinal cord, nerves (control, sensation)
  • Endocrine — glands secreting hormones (slow, body-wide regulation)
  • Cardiovascular — heart, blood, vessels (transport)
  • Lymphatic/Immune — lymph nodes, white blood cells (defence)
  • Respiratory — lungs, airways (gas exchange)
  • Digestive — gut, liver, pancreas (nutrient extraction)
  • Urinary — kidneys, bladder (waste excretion, fluid balance)
  • Reproductive — gonads, associated structures

title: The Cardiovascular System
description: How the heart and blood vessels supply every cell in the body

concepts.title: The Heart
concepts.contentHtml:
The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist. It has four chambers: two atria (upper, receiving) and two ventricles (lower, pumping). The right side receives deoxygenated blood and sends it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body.

Heart valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic) prevent backflow. The lub-dub heartbeat sound is the valves snapping shut.

The heart's electrical conduction system coordinates contraction. The sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker, firing ~60–100 times per minute at rest. Its electrical signal triggers atrial contraction, then passes through the AV node to the ventricles.

concepts.title: Blood Vessels and Circulation
concepts.contentHtml:
Blood travels in a closed loop: heart → arteries (carry oxygenated blood away from heart, thick-walled, pulsatile) → arterioles → capillaries (single-cell walls; site of gas, nutrient, and waste exchange) → venules → veins (return blood to heart, thin-walled, valves prevent backflow).

The cardiovascular system has two circuits: pulmonary (heart ↔ lungs) and systemic (heart ↔ rest of body). William Harvey described circulation in 1628 — one of the most important discoveries in medicine.

Blood pressure is measured as systolic/diastolic (e.g. 120/80 mmHg). Systolic is peak pressure during heart contraction; diastolic is pressure when the heart relaxes.

concepts.title: Blood: Composition and Function
concepts.contentHtml:
Blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix (plasma) and cellular elements.

  • Red blood cells (erythrocytes): carry oxygen via haemoglobin; biconcave discs; no nucleus; 4–5 million per mm³
  • White blood cells (leukocytes): immune defence; ~7,000 per mm³; several types (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes...)
  • Platelets (thrombocytes): clotting; ~250,000 per mm³; fragments of megakaryocytes

Plasma contains water, proteins (albumin, antibodies, clotting factors), glucose, ions, and dissolved gases. Blood volume is ~5 litres in an adult. The heart pumps this entire volume roughly once per minute at rest.

title: The Respiratory and Digestive Systems
description: Gas exchange in the lungs and nutrient extraction in the gut

concepts.title: The Respiratory System
concepts.contentHtml:
The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and expels CO2. Air flows: nose/mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

Alveoli are tiny air sacs (~300 million in each lung) with walls just one cell thick. Surrounded by capillaries, they are the site of gas exchange by diffusion: O2 moves from air into blood (high to low concentration); CO2 moves out.

The total alveolar surface area is ~70 m² — the size of a tennis court. Surfactant (produced by type II alveolar cells) reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Premature babies lack surfactant — a life-threatening problem treated with artificial surfactant.

concepts.title: The Digestive System
concepts.contentHtml:
The digestive system breaks food into absorbable molecules and excretes waste.

Mechanical digestion: chewing, stomach churning. Chemical digestion: enzymes break down polymers. Salivary amylase starts starch digestion; stomach acid (pH 2) and pepsin attack proteins; pancreatic enzymes complete digestion; bile (from liver, stored in gallbladder) emulsifies fats.

Absorption mainly occurs in the small intestine: folds, villi, and microvilli create ~250 m² of absorptive surface. Nutrients enter blood (carbohydrates, proteins, water-soluble vitamins) or lymph (fats). The large intestine absorbs water and houses the gut microbiome.

concepts.title: The Liver — The Body's Chemistry Lab
concepts.contentHtml:
The liver is the largest internal organ (~1.4 kg) and performs over 500 known functions. It is the master metabolic integrator of the body.

Key functions: glucose homeostasis (stores glycogen when blood glucose is high; releases glucose when low), detoxification (processes alcohol, drugs, metabolic wastes), protein synthesis (produces albumin, clotting factors), bile production (fat digestion), cholesterol metabolism.

All blood from the intestines passes through the hepatic portal vein to the liver before reaching general circulation. This means the liver gets first access to absorbed nutrients — and first exposure to ingested toxins. The liver can regenerate: up to 75% can be surgically removed and it will regrow.

title: The Nervous and Endocrine Systems
description: Fast electrical signalling vs. slow hormonal control

concepts.title: The Nervous System
concepts.contentHtml:
The nervous system provides rapid, targeted communication via electrical signals. It is divided into the central nervous system (CNS: brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS: all nerves outside the CNS).

The PNS has two functional divisions: somatic (voluntary control of skeletal muscles) and autonomic (involuntary control of viscera). The autonomic system is further split: sympathetic (fight-or-flight: accelerates heart, dilates airways, redirects blood to muscles) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest: slows heart, promotes digestion).

A reflex arc — sensory receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector — operates without involving the brain, enabling fast protective responses.

concepts.title: The Endocrine System
concepts.contentHtml:
The endocrine system uses hormones — chemical messengers secreted directly into the bloodstream — for slow, sustained, body-wide coordination.

Major glands: hypothalamus (master controller; links nervous and endocrine systems), pituitary (releases hormones that regulate other glands), thyroid (metabolic rate), adrenal glands (cortisol for stress; adrenaline for emergency), pancreas (insulin and glucagon for blood glucose), gonads (sex hormones).

Hormone action is slow (minutes to hours vs. milliseconds for nerves) but long-lasting and widespread. The same hormone can affect many organs simultaneously. The nervous and endocrine systems constantly interact — stress triggers both nerve impulses and cortisol release.

concepts.title: The Immune System
concepts.contentHtml:
The immune system defends against pathogens. It has two arms.

Innate immunity is fast and non-specific: physical barriers (skin, mucus), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages eat pathogens), inflammation (increased blood flow, immune cell recruitment), and fever (higher temperature inhibits pathogen growth).

Adaptive immunity is slow (~1–2 weeks) but specific and has memory. B cells produce antibodies — proteins that bind specific antigens on pathogens. T cells coordinate responses and directly kill infected cells.

After infection, memory cells persist. Second exposure triggers a faster, stronger response — this is the basis of vaccination. Edward Jenner's 1796 cowpox vaccination against smallpox was the first successful vaccine.

title: The Musculoskeletal System
description: Bones, muscles, and how the body moves

concepts.title: The Skeletal System
concepts.contentHtml:
The adult human skeleton has 206 bones. Functions: support (framework for soft tissues), protection (skull for brain, ribcage for heart and lungs), movement (levers for muscles to act on), haematopoiesis (red bone marrow produces blood cells), mineral storage (99% of body calcium is in bone).

Bone is living tissue, constantly remodelled by osteoblasts (build bone) and osteoclasts (break it down). Bone density peaks in early adulthood and gradually declines — physical activity, calcium, and vitamin D maintain it. Osteoporosis is pathological bone loss, common in post-menopausal women.

Joints connect bones: fibrous (skull sutures), cartilaginous (vertebral discs), and synovial (freely moveable — knee, shoulder).

concepts.title: Muscle Contraction
concepts.contentHtml:
Skeletal muscle fibres are packed with myofibrils made of alternating thick filaments (myosin) and thin filaments (actin). The sliding filament theory (Huxley and Hanson, 1954) explains contraction: myosin heads attach to actin, pull the thin filaments inward, and the sarcomere (the basic contractile unit) shortens.

A nerve impulse releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, triggering an action potential in the muscle fibre. This releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which enables myosin heads to bind actin.

Muscle contraction requires ATP at every step. Fatigue occurs when ATP cannot be regenerated fast enough — whether from lactic acid buildup in intense exercise or glycogen depletion in endurance events.

concepts.title: Kidneys and Fluid Balance
concepts.contentHtml:
The kidneys are the body's filtration and regulation organs — they maintain blood composition, fluid balance, and pH.

Each kidney contains ~1 million nephrons, the functional units. Blood is filtered under pressure in the glomerulus; the filtrate passes through the tubule where useful substances (glucose, most water, ions) are reabsorbed and waste products (urea, creatinine, excess ions) remain.

The hormone ADH (antidiuretic hormone) controls water reabsorption: high ADH → concentrated urine; low ADH → dilute urine. Aldosterone regulates sodium reabsorption and blood pressure. Dialysis substitutes kidney function when kidneys fail by filtering blood through an artificial membrane.

title: The Immune & Lymphatic System
description: Body's defenses and circulation of immune cells

concepts.title: Lymphatic Anatomy
concepts.contentHtml:
The lymphatic system is a one-way drainage network. Lymphatic capillaries collect interstitial fluid (lymph) from tissues; vessels return it to the bloodstream via the thoracic duct.

Lymph nodes are filter stations along the way — bean-sized structures full of B and T cells. Pathogens trapped here trigger immune responses (and palpably swollen 'glands' when you're sick).

Other lymphoid organs: spleen (filters blood, recycles old red cells), thymus (T-cell maturation), tonsils, bone marrow (produces all immune cells), gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT — Peyer's patches).

concepts.title: Why It Matters Anatomically
concepts.contentHtml:
Lymphatic vessels are also conduits for cancer metastasis — many tumors spread first to nearby lymph nodes. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is a standard part of breast cancer surgical staging.

Lymphedema (impaired lymph drainage) causes chronic swelling — common after axillary lymph node removal in breast cancer treatment. Massage and compression therapy help; surgical reconstructions are improving.

The lymphatic system has been called the 'forgotten circulation' but is increasingly studied for its roles in immunity, fluid balance, fat absorption, and disease.

concepts.title: Brain Glymphatic System
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades the brain was thought to have no lymphatic system. In 2012 Maiken Nedergaard's lab discovered the glymphatic system — perivascular spaces that flush waste from the brain, especially during sleep.

This is one reason sleep is so essential: glymphatic clearance of metabolic waste (including amyloid-β) ramps up during slow-wave sleep. Disrupted clearance may contribute to Alzheimer's.

The brain's meningeal lymphatic vessels were also rediscovered in 2015 — overturning a century of textbook teaching that the CNS had no lymphatic drainage.

title: Reproductive System
description: Anatomy of how new humans are made

concepts.title: Male Reproductive Anatomy
concepts.contentHtml:
Testes produce sperm and testosterone. Sperm travel through the epididymis (matured here), vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, and urethra. Accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral) add fluid components forming semen.

The testes' location outside the body keeps them ~2 °C cooler than core — needed for spermatogenesis. Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) causes reduced fertility and elevated cancer risk if not corrected.

concepts.title: Female Reproductive Anatomy
concepts.contentHtml:
Ovaries produce eggs and sex hormones. Fallopian tubes carry eggs from ovary to uterus and are the typical site of fertilization. Uterus houses developing fetus. Cervix opens to vagina.

The menstrual cycle integrates ovarian, uterine, and pituitary hormone changes. Ovulation occurs ~14 days before next menstruation. Days fertile span ~6 days centered on ovulation (sperm survive ~5 days; egg ~24 hours).

concepts.title: Pregnancy and Birth
concepts.contentHtml:
Fertilization in the fallopian tube → blastocyst → implants in uterine wall → placenta develops. The placenta is the interface for gas, nutrient, and waste exchange between mother and fetus, and produces hormones (HCG, progesterone, estrogen).

Birth (parturition) involves cervical ripening, uterine contractions, fetal expulsion, and placental delivery. Hormonal cascade with oxytocin (induces contractions) and prostaglandins (cervical ripening) at the center.

Cesarean sections account for ~30% of US births — more than the WHO 'optimal' rate of 10-15%. The reasons are complex: maternal age, obesity, malpractice fears, induction practices.

title: Modern Anatomy: Imaging & Beyond
description: How we see the body now

concepts.title: X-ray, CT, MRI
concepts.contentHtml:
X-rays attenuate based on density — bones absorb, soft tissue passes. Cheap, fast, ideal for fractures and chest screening. Some radiation dose.

CT (computed tomography) uses many X-rays from different angles, computer-reconstructed into 3D. Higher dose, but excellent anatomical detail.

MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) exploits hydrogen nuclei in tissues. Strong magnetic field plus radiofrequency pulses → detailed soft-tissue contrast without ionizing radiation. Slow and expensive but unmatched for many applications.

concepts.title: Ultrasound & Functional Imaging
concepts.contentHtml:
Ultrasound: sound waves bounce off tissue interfaces. No radiation, real-time, portable, cheap. Mainstay of obstetrics and emergency medicine.

PET uses positron-emitting tracers to visualize metabolism — cancer cells use lots of glucose; ¹⁸F-FDG-PET highlights them. Combined with CT (PET-CT) for anatomical context.

fMRI tracks blood oxygenation as a proxy for neural activity. Reveals brain function during cognitive tasks — has transformed neuroscience.

concepts.title: AI in Imaging
concepts.contentHtml:
AI models now read medical images at expert level for many specific tasks. Mammography lesion detection, diabetic retinopathy from fundus photos, skin cancer from dermoscopy.

Several systems are FDA-cleared. Radiology is being automated for screening tasks while remaining heavily human-led for complex diagnoses.

Concerns: bias from training-data demographics, generalization to new populations, integration into clinical workflow. Promise: scaling expert-level diagnosis to underserved areas.
